findings.title: Restarted process gets a fresh SpansBuffer, losing state and mixing up metrics
findings.body: `_create_process_for_shards` builds a new `SpansBuffer(shards)` on every restart and overwrites `self.buffers[process_index]`. Any in-memory state held by the old buffer is lost, such as the `any_shard_at_limit` flag and the stored-segment metrics used by `record_stored_segments`. The old process is also only killed if it is a `multiprocessing.Process`. In thread mode, a hung thread is left running next to its replacement, so two flushers then flush the same shards.

findings.title: Restart counter never resets and restart limit is off by one
findings.body: `process_restarts` is only ever incremented, so a process that restarts occasionally over a long uptime eventually exceeds MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS and crashes the whole consumer. The check uses `>` before incrementing, so 11 restarts are allowed rather than 10. This was already the behaviour before the PR, but with several processes the chance of reaching the limit is higher.

findings.title: join with a timeout can skip terminating processes
findings.body: In `join()`, when the deadline passes the loop `break`s before reaching `process.terminate()`. The remaining processes, and the current one if it is still alive, are never terminated. They are left running after shutdown or rebalance and hold Redis and Kafka resources until the daemon flag kills them at interpreter exit. The `join` timeout is also used as a single budget across all processes, so later processes get no time.

findings.title: Inconsistent metric tag name
findings.body: The `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` timer and the `segment_size_bytes` metric use the tag `shard`, but `wait_produce` uses `shards`. This splits dashboards and queries for what is the same dimension. The tag values are also comma-joined shard lists, which makes cardinality grow with the shard assignment.

findings.title: Test relies on real sleeps, and the new test only checks the process map
findings.body: `test_basic` calls `time.sleep(0.1)` after `time.sleep` has been monkeypatched to a no-op, so it does not actually wait. It is therefore not a real synchronisation point and can be flaky. `test_flusher_processes_limit` only checks the process-to-shard mapping. It does not test that flushing works with multiple processes, or that unhealthy-process restarts and backpressure behave correctly across them.
